CausalChain: Fibrotic liver → Increased matrix stiffness → Activation of integrin β5–FAK–MEK/ERK signaling in TAMs → Upregulation of HIF‐1α → Mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS accumulation → Activation of TGF‐β signaling → M2 TAM polarization → Suppression of anti‐tumor CD8⁺ T cell activity
Hypothesis: In HCC developing in fibrotic, stiff livers, targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in TAMs—by disrupting mechanosensitive signaling pathways—can shift TAMs from an immunosuppressive M2 state to a pro‐inflammatory M1 phenotype, thereby enhancing anti‐tumor immune responses and the efficacy of immunotherapies.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) often arises in fibrotic or cirrhotic livers, where increased tissue stiffness alters cellular signaling. Recent studies indicate that the mechanical properties of the liver tumor microenvironment not only affect the behavior of cancer cells, but also modulate the phenotype of tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs). In this context, we propose that matrix stiffness activates mechanotransductive pathways (such as the integrin β5–FAK–MEK/ERK axis), leading to upregulation of hypoxia inducible factor‐1α (HIF‐1α) in TAMs. This, in turn, promotes mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, triggering TGF‐β signaling and the skewing of TAMs toward an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype. By targeting mitochondrial dysfunction within TAMs, it may be possible to reverse their polarization, re‐establish pro‐inflammatory (M1) properties, and ultimately restore effective CD8⁺ T cell–mediated anti‐tumor responses in HCC.
